items.prompt: Which enzyme adds new nucleotides to a growing DNA strand during replication?

options.label: RNA polymerase
DNA ligase
Helicase
DNA polymerase

rubric: DNA polymerase synthesises the new strand by adding nucleotides.
Ligase only seals nicks, and helicase only unwinds the helix.

items.prompt: Which codon is the usual start codon that begins translation in eukaryotes?

options.label: UGA
GGC
AUG
UAA

rubric: AUG codes for methionine and signals the start of translation.
UAA and UGA are stop codons.

items.prompt: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?

options.label: Guanine
Adenine
Uracil
Thymine

rubric: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.
Thymine is the DNA-only base, which is the common mix-up.

items.prompt: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix at the replication fork?

options.label: Primase
Topoisomerase I
Helicase
DNA ligase

rubric: Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between strands to unwind the helix.
Primase makes RNA primers and ligase joins fragments.

items.prompt: Which molecule brings amino acids to the ribosome during translation?

options.label: tRNA
DNA
rRNA
mRNA

rubric: tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon.
mRNA carries the message and rRNA is part of the ribosome.

items.prompt: Which of these are required components of a standard PCR reaction mixture? Select all that apply.

options.label: Free nucleotides (dNTPs)
DNA ligase
Heat-stable DNA polymerase
Primers
Ribosomes

rubric: PCR needs a heat-stable polymerase, primers and dNTPs plus template DNA.
Ligase and ribosomes are not part of PCR.

items.prompt: A student wants to cut a plasmid at one specific DNA sequence so a gene can be inserted. The lab technician hands over a tube labelled with an enzyme that recognises short sequences and cuts DNA there. Which type of enzyme is this?

options.label: Restriction endonuclease
RNA polymerase
Reverse transcriptase
Helicase

rubric: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific recognition sequences.
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA, not cuts at sites.

items.prompt: Why is DNA replication described as semiconservative?

options.label: Each new helix has one original strand and one new strand
The original helix stays intact and a separate new copy is made
Half of the genome is copied and the other half is skipped
Each new double helix is made of two entirely new strands

rubric: Semiconservative means each daughter helix keeps one parental strand.
Other options describe conservative or partial copying.

items.prompt: Why does each PCR cycle begin with a high-temperature step of about 95 °C?

options.label: To separate the two template strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
To activate the heat-stable polymerase so it can start extending
To let primers join to the template strands at their complementary sites
To join the new strands to the template with covalent bonds

rubric: Heat denatures the double strands so primers can bind later.
Primer binding happens at the lower annealing temperature.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly describes transcription?

options.label: A DNA molecule is copied before cell division
An RNA is converted into DNA by an enzyme
A protein is built from an mRNA on a ribosome
An RNA copy is made from a DNA template

rubric: Transcription makes RNA using DNA as a template.
Building protein is translation and copying DNA is replication.

items.prompt: A point mutation changes a codon in the middle of a gene into a stop codon. What is the most likely result?

options.label: A shortened protein that ends early
No change, because the code is degenerate
A longer protein with extra amino acids
A normal protein with one amino acid swapped

rubric: A premature stop codon ends translation early, giving a truncated protein.
Degeneracy covers changes between codons for the same amino acid, not stop codons.

items.prompt: In E. coli with no lactose present, why are the lac operon genes mostly off?

options.label: The repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase
The genes are physically deleted until lactose appears again
RNA polymerase cannot bind the cell's DNA without lactose present
The repressor is bound to lactose and so cannot act on DNA

rubric: Without lactose the repressor sits on the operator and blocks transcription.
Lactose (allolactose) removes the repressor to switch the genes on.

items.prompt: Which statements about the genetic code are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each codon is three nucleotides long
The code is nearly the same in almost all organisms
Several different codons can code for the same amino acid
One codon can code for several different amino acids
Stop codons each code for a specific amino acid

rubric: The code is triplet, degenerate and nearly universal.
Codons are unambiguous, and stop codons code for no amino acid.

items.prompt: A researcher inserts a human gene into a plasmid that also carries an ampicillin resistance gene. She transforms bacteria with it and spreads them on agar containing ampicillin. Why does she use ampicillin plates?

options.label: It lets only bacteria that took up the plasmid grow
It cuts the plasmid so the gene can be inserted
It switches on the human gene inside the bacteria
It makes the bacteria copy the inserted gene faster

rubric: Ampicillin selects for cells carrying the resistance gene on the plasmid.
It does not cut DNA, speed copying or activate the inserted gene.

items.prompt: DNA replication is described as semiconservative. What does this mean for each of the two DNA molecules made from one parent helix?

options.label: Each is a mosaic of short original and short new segments
Each contains one original strand and one newly made strand
One has both original strands and the other has both new
Each contains two newly made strands only

rubric: Semiconservative means each daughter helix keeps one parental strand as template and gains one new strand.
Distractors describe conservative and dispersive models.

items.prompt: Which requirement applies to DNA polymerase when it starts copying, but not to RNA polymerase when it starts transcribing?

options.label: A template strand to read
A primer providing a free 3' end
A promoter sequence to bind
Nucleoside triphosphates as building blocks

rubric: DNA polymerase can only extend an existing 3' end, so it needs a primer; RNA polymerase starts chains de novo.
Other options apply to both enzymes or to transcription only.

items.prompt: What is the role of a codon in translation?

options.label: It is an rRNA region that joins amino acids by peptide bonds
It is a DNA triplet that signals where replication starts
It is an mRNA triplet specifying one amino acid or a stop
It is a tRNA region that binds an amino acid

rubric: A codon is a three-nucleotide mRNA unit read by the ribosome to specify an amino acid or stop.
The distractors confuse codons with the anticodon/acceptor end, origins, and rRNA catalytic function.

items.prompt: In E. coli, why are lac operon genes transcribed when lactose is present and glucose is absent?

options.label: Lactose enters the ribosome, which raises translation of mRNA
Lactose cuts the operator DNA, which removes the block
Allolactose binds the repressor, which then leaves the operator
Lactose binds the promoter and recruits RNA polymerase to it

rubric: The inducer allolactose binds the repressor, changing its shape so it releases the operator and allows transcription.
Distractors give the inducer roles it does not have.

items.prompt: Why is Taq polymerase commonly used in PCR instead of a typical human DNA polymerase?

options.label: It is heat stable and survives the denaturation step
It proofreads more accurately than other polymerases
It works at low temperature so DNA stays annealed
It copies DNA without needing any primers

rubric: Taq comes from a heat-loving bacterium and is not destroyed by ~95 C denaturation, so it can be used for many cycles.
Distractors misstate primer need, fidelity and temperature.

items.prompt: Which events occur during processing of a eukaryotic pre-mRNA before it is translated? Select all that apply.

options.label: Introns are removed by splicing
A poly-A tail is added at the 3' end
A Shine-Dalgarno sequence is added for ribosome binding
A 5' cap is added to the transcript

rubric: Capping, polyadenylation and splicing are the standard eukaryotic processing steps.
Shine-Dalgarno sequences are bacterial and are encoded in the gene, not added.

items.prompt: A student studies a replication fork. One new strand is made as a continuous piece toward the fork, while the other is made in short pieces called Okazaki fragments. The student asks why the second strand must be made in pieces. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: The second template strand is RNA so it must be copied in pieces
Ligase prevents long strands from forming on one template
DNA polymerase only adds nucleotides 5' to 3', so the strand running away from the fork is made in segments
Helicase can only unwind a short stretch at a time

rubric: Polymerase extends only 3' ends, and the antiparallel template forces one strand to be made discontinuously as the fork opens.
Distractors invoke helicase, ligase or RNA templates incorrectly.

items.prompt: A template DNA strand reads 3'-TACGGT-5'. What is the mRNA transcribed from it, written 5' to 3'?

options.label: 5'-ACCGUA-3'
5'-AUGCCA-3'
5'-ATGCCA-3'
5'-UACGGU-3'

rubric: Complementary pairing gives 5'-AUGCCA-3' (A-U, T-A, G-C, C-G).
Distractors keep T, copy the template directly, or forget the reversed direction.

items.prompt: An mRNA reads 5'-GCAUGGCUUAACGA-3'. Translation starts at the first AUG. Assuming UAA is a stop codon, how many amino acids are in the peptide?
rubric: Reading from AUG: AUG GCU UAA gives Met-Ala then stop, so 2 amino acids.
Other counts include the stop or start translation at the wrong place.

items.prompt: One double-stranded DNA template undergoes 5 perfect PCR cycles. How many double-stranded DNA molecules exist at the end?
rubric: Each cycle doubles the molecule number, so 2^5 = 32.
Distractors add or multiply cycles instead of doubling.

items.prompt: A plasmid is cut with EcoRI. Which fragment can be ligated into the cut site using only DNA ligase?

options.label: A fragment cut with EcoRI, leaving matching sticky ends
A fragment cut with a different enzyme with other overhangs
A fragment amplified by PCR with no cutting
A fragment cut with a different enzyme leaving blunt ends

rubric: EcoRI ends have compatible sticky overhangs that base-pair and can be sealed by ligase.
Other options have non-matching ends or no ends prepared.

items.prompt: A mutation changes the codon GAA to GAG. Both codons specify glutamate. What is the effect on the protein?

options.label: A silent change with no amino acid difference
A nonsense change that ends the protein early
A frameshift that changes all later amino acids
A missense change that replaces glutamate

rubric: The substitution gives the same amino acid, so it is silent.
Distractors confuse substitutions with frameshift, missense and nonsense effects.

items.prompt: In E. coli, which mutations would cause the lac genes to be transcribed even when lactose is absent? Select all that apply.

options.label: A deletion of the lacZ coding sequence
An operator mutation that stops the repressor binding
A mutation that inactivates the lacI repressor protein
A promoter mutation that blocks RNA polymerase binding

rubric: Without a functional repressor or its binding site, the operon is constitutively on.
A lacZ deletion removes one gene, and a promoter defect would reduce transcription.

items.prompt: A student ligates a gene into the lacZ region of a plasmid and transforms E. coli. The cells are plated on ampicillin and X-gal, where lacZ produces blue colonies. Colonies grow, some blue and some white. Which colonies most likely carry the plasmid with the insert?

options.label: Blue colonies, since an intact lacZ shows the insert is present
White colonies, since they lack plasmid and resist ampicillin
White colonies, since the insert likely disrupted lacZ
Blue colonies, since only they can grow on ampicillin

rubric: Insertion into lacZ stops functional beta-galactosidase, so colonies with insert stay white while growing on ampicillin.
Distractors misread blue as insert-positive or say that white cells lack plasmid.

items.prompt: A template strand reads 3'-TACGGATC-5'. Which mRNA sequence is transcribed from it?

options.label: 5'-ATGCCTAG-3'
5'-GAUCCGUA-3'
5'-UACGGAUC-3'
5'-AUGCCUAG-3'

rubric: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template, with U replacing T, giving 5'-AUGCCUAG-3'.
Distractors copy the template, reverse it without complementing, or use T instead of U.

items.prompt: A PCR starts with 100 double-stranded template molecules and runs 6 cycles at ideal efficiency. How many double-stranded copies of the target exist at the end?
rubric: Ideal PCR doubles each cycle: 100 x 2^6 = 6,400.
Distractors use linear addition (600) or the wrong power of two.

items.prompt: A circular 4,000 bp plasmid has EcoRI sites at positions 500 and 1,700. Which fragment sizes result from a complete EcoRI digest?

options.label: 500 bp and 1,700 bp
1,700 bp and 2,300 bp
1,200 bp and 2,800 bp

rubric: A circular molecule cut at two sites gives two fragments: 1,700-500 = 1,200 bp and 4,000-1,200 = 2,800 bp.
Distractors treat the plasmid as linear or use the site positions as fragment sizes.

items.prompt: A bacterial mRNA reads 5'-GGAUGGCUUAAGC-3'. Translation starts at the first AUG. How many amino acids are in the resulting peptide?
rubric: Reading from AUG: AUG (Met), GCU (Ala), UAA (stop), so the peptide has 2 amino acids.
Distractors count the stop codon or start reading from the first nucleotide.

items.prompt: E. coli with a normal lac operon grow in medium containing lactose and a high concentration of glucose. What do you predict for lacZ expression?

options.label: Low, because glucose keeps cAMP low so CAP cannot activate, even though the repressor is released
High, because lactose inactivates the repressor and nothing else limits transcription of the operon
Low, because glucose binds the repressor and holds it on the operator despite lactose being present
High, because glucose is a stronger inducer than lactose and further boosts transcription of the operon

rubric: High glucose lowers cAMP, so CAP-cAMP does not bind and transcription stays low despite repressor release.
Distractors ignore catabolite repression or invent glucose binding the repressor.

items.prompt: You are designing a primer pair to amplify a 500 bp target by PCR. Which design features are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.label: The 3' ends of the two primers lack complementarity to each other, which limits primer-dimer formation
Each primer is designed to end in a long run of G and C bases at its 3' end, so that binding is strong enough to tolerate any annealing temperature
Each primer's 3' end pairs with opposite strands flanking the target, with the primers pointing toward each other
The two primers have similar melting temperatures so a single annealing temperature suits both

rubric: Facing primers on opposite strands, matched Tm and no 3' complementarity are standard design rules.
Identical primers would bind only one strand and give no exponential amplification of the target.

items.prompt: You ligate a PCR fragment into the multiple cloning site inside lacZα of a plasmid carrying ampR. You transform lacZΔM15 E. coli and plate on ampicillin, X-gal and IPTG. Which colonies most likely carry plasmid with an insert?

options.label: Blue colonies, because the insert adds a new open reading frame that activates X-gal cleavage
No colonies, because IPTG blocks replication of any plasmid that has acquired an insert
White colonies, because the insert disrupts lacZα so no functional β-galactosidase cleaves X-gal
Blue colonies, because growth on ampicillin shows the plasmid is present and so it must contain the insert

rubric: Insertion into lacZα prevents alpha-complementation, so recombinant colonies stay white on X-gal.
Blue colonies carry plasmid with intact lacZα; ampicillin resistance only shows plasmid uptake, not insertion.

items.prompt: A PCR with two 20-nt primers gives a strong band near 40 bp and only a faint band at the expected 800 bp. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Too much template DNA, which forces the polymerase to terminate early on every cycle of extension
Primer-dimer formed through complementary 3' ends, which polymerase extends and amplifies instead of the target
Too high an annealing temperature, which lets primers bind the target at many off-target sites
Excess extension time, which makes the polymerase cut the long target into short fragments during cycling

rubric: A small product about the size of two primers indicates primer-dimer from 3' complementarity consuming primers.
Distractors misattribute small products to extension time, high stringency or template excess.

items.prompt: In RT-PCR for an intron-containing gene, primers lie within a single exon. The +RT sample and the no-RT control both give the same-size band. What does this indicate?

options.label: Contaminating genomic DNA served as template, so DNase treatment or intron-spanning primers are needed
The mRNA is so abundant that it is amplified directly by Taq polymerase without reverse transcription
The primers form dimers that happen to match the expected product size in both reactions
The reverse transcriptase is active without added enzyme, so the control is uninformative about cDNA synthesis

rubric: Product without RT must come from DNA; primers in one exon cannot tell cDNA from genomic DNA.
Distractors suggest RT activity in the control or that Taq amplifies RNA directly.

items.prompt: A bacterial gene mutant shows a normal-sized, normally abundant mRNA on a northern blot, but protein is reduced 20-fold. Which mutation best explains this?

options.label: A deletion of the -10 promoter element, which lowers initiation of transcription by RNA polymerase
A mutation in the terminator hairpin, which lets RNA polymerase read through and make longer transcripts
A mutation in the operator, which prevents the repressor from releasing the DNA in response to inducer
A change in the Shine-Dalgarno sequence, which weakens ribosome binding on an otherwise normal transcript

rubric: Normal mRNA size and level point to a translation-initiation defect such as a weakened Shine-Dalgarno site.
The other options would alter transcript level or length, which is not observed.

items.prompt: A vector is cut with EcoRI alone and ligated with an EcoRI-cut insert. The vector-only ligation control (no insert) gives nearly as many colonies as the full ligation. What is the best explanation?

options.label: EcoRI star activity has cut the vector at random sites, producing many fragments that reseal into new plasmids
Ampicillin selection is failing, so cells without any plasmid grow on the plate in both cases
The insert is too large to ligate, so the ligase joins vector ends to each other in both reactions
The vector's compatible ends retain 5' phosphates and recircularize, so dephosphorylation or two enzymes is needed

rubric: A single-enzyme digest gives compatible phosphorylated ends that self-ligate; phosphatase or directional cloning prevents this.
Distractors blame selection failure or ligation artifacts that would not give plasmid-bearing colonies in the vector-only control.

items.prompt: An E. coli partial diploid has a chromosome that is lacI- lacZ+ and an F' plasmid that is lacI+ lacZ-. No lactose is present. What is β-galactosidase expression, and why?

options.label: Not made, because diffusible repressor from the plasmid lacI+ gene binds the chromosomal operator in trans
Made constitutively, because chromosomal lacI- cannot be rescued by repressor made from another DNA molecule
Made at a low basal level, because the plasmid lacZ- allele is dominant over the chromosomal lacZ+ allele
Made when glucose is absent, because the plasmid lacZ- allele blocks the chromosomal gene at other times

rubric: lacI encodes a diffusible repressor acting in trans, so the plasmid copy represses the chromosomal lacZ+ without lactose.
Distractors treat lacI as cis-acting or invent dominance of lacZ-.

items.prompt: A DNA polymerase mutant lacks its 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease but is otherwise intact. Which observations are expected? Select all that apply.

options.label: Polymerization still proceeds 5'→3' because the polymerase active site is separate from the exonuclease site
Only deletions and never base substitutions accumulate because the exonuclease prevents slippage
Replication cannot initiate because proofreading is required to load the helicase at the origin
Mismatched nucleotides stay in the new strand more often, raising the substitution rate
RNA primers on the lagging strand are no longer removed because proofreading excises the primers

rubric: Loss of proofreading raises error rate while 5'→3' synthesis continues through the separate polymerase site.
Primer removal and helicase loading are separate functions; the 'only deletions' claim is unsupported.

items.prompt: In a patient's cells, a eukaryotic gene gives an mRNA about 150 nt shorter than normal and a slightly smaller, in-frame protein. Genomic sequencing shows a G to A change at the invariant AG at the 3' end of intron 4. Exon 5 is 150 nt long. Which explanation best fits?

options.label: Transcription terminates early at the mutation, producing a short pre-mRNA that is polyadenylated
The change creates a premature stop codon in exon 5, so the ribosome stops before the protein is made
The 3' splice site of intron 4 is lost, so exon 5 is skipped and exon 4 joins exon 6
The poly(A) signal is destroyed, so the mRNA is degraded from the 3' end and loses 150 nt

rubric: Loss of the intron's 3' splice acceptor commonly causes exon skipping; skipping a 150 nt exon gives a shorter in-frame product.
The other options would not produce a precise 150 nt deletion in a mature in-frame transcript.

items.prompt: A PCR with two primers gives no product, although the positive-control template and primer pair work in the same run. The primers have calculated Tm values of 72 C and 54 C, and the annealing step was set at 68 C. Which diagnosis best explains the failure?

options.label: The 54 C primer cannot anneal at 68 C, so exponential amplification never starts
The extension step is too short, so polymerase drops off every template strand
The denaturation step is too hot, so the primers are destroyed before annealing
The 72 C primer is too stable, so it blocks polymerase from extending at 68 C

rubric: Annealing at 68 C is far above the lower-Tm primer's Tm, so only one strand is primed and no exponential product forms.
Distractors blame the high-Tm primer or the cycling steps, ignoring the Tm mismatch.

items.prompt: An E. coli merodiploid carries a chromosomal lacO+ lacZ+ and an F' plasmid with a lacO^c (operator-constitutive) mutation upstream of a nonfunctional lacZ-. Lac repressor is normal. No lactose or IPTG is present. What is observed for beta-galactosidase activity?

options.label: None, because the lacZ- allele is dominant and inactivates the wild-type enzyme
High, because the O^c mutation acts in trans on every lacZ copy in the cell
High, because the O^c mutation titrates repressor away from the chromosomal operator
None, because the O^c mutation acts only in cis and the chromosomal lacZ+ stays repressed

rubric: Operator mutations affect only the genes on the same DNA molecule, so the O^c lacZ- copy is constitutive but nonfunctional.
Distractors treat the operator as a diffusible trans-acting factor or invoke dominance.

items.prompt: A temperature-sensitive mutant E. coli strain is shifted to the nonpermissive temperature during replication. Pulse-labelled DNA shows many short fragments of about 1000 nt that are never joined into long strands, while the leading strand is synthesised normally. Which defective component best explains this?

options.label: DNA gyrase, so positive supercoils ahead of the fork halt synthesis
DNA ligase, so nicks between lagging-strand fragments stay unsealed
Helicase, so the parental duplex stays closed and starves both strands
Single-strand binding protein, so the leading template collapses into hairpins

rubric: Short unjoined lagging-strand fragments with normal leading-strand synthesis point to a failure to seal nicks, i.e. ligase.
Helicase or gyrase defects would stall both strands, not only join lagging fragments.

items.prompt: A patient's gene has a point mutation changing the invariant GU at the 5' end of intron 3 to CU. RT-PCR of mRNA shows products of abnormal size. Which mechanism best accounts for the abnormal products?

options.label: The mutation changes the reading frame in the 5' UTR, so the 5' cap is not added
The mutation creates a new polyadenylation signal, so the transcript ends in intron 3
The mutation blocks RNA polymerase II elongation, giving truncated transcripts only
The spliceosome cannot recognise the donor site, causing exon skipping or intron retention

rubric: The GU donor is essential for U1 snRNP recognition, so its loss disrupts splicing of that intron.
Distractors assign the defect to elongation, capping or polyadenylation, which do not depend on this dinucleotide.

items.prompt: A vector is digested with only EcoRI, an insert is ligated in, and the mix is transformed into cells plated on ampicillin, X-gal and IPTG. Nearly every colony is blue. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: The vector re-ligated to itself because single-enzyme ends were not dephosphorylated
The ampicillin was inactive, so cells without any plasmid grew into colonies
The IPTG concentration was too high, so it blocked lacZ-alpha transcription
The insert was ligated in the wrong orientation, so lacZ-alpha is still intact

rubric: Blue colonies mean lacZ-alpha is intact; a single-enzyme cut with compatible ends lets the vector re-close unless it is dephosphorylated.
Orientation of an insert does not restore lacZ-alpha, and failed antibiotic selection would give many white background colonies.

items.prompt: In a cell line, RT-qPCR shows normal levels of mRNA for gene X, yet a Western blot shows almost no X protein. Which of the following could explain this result? Select all that apply.

options.label: The X promoter was deleted, so no X transcripts are made in the cells
A mutation changed the start codon context so ribosomes rarely initiate translation
The X protein is ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome within minutes
A microRNA that represses translation of X mRNA is strongly expressed
An enhancer for X was lost, which should give low mRNA levels

rubric: Translational repression, poor initiation and rapid degradation reduce protein without lowering mRNA.
Loss of the promoter or enhancer would reduce mRNA, contradicting the RT-qPCR result.

items.prompt: A lab fuses a series of 5' deletions of a gene's upstream region to a luciferase reporter and transfects each into cells. Constructs from -1000 down to -500 give similar low activity. Deleting from -500 to -300 raises activity fivefold, and removing -300 to -100 drops activity back to near zero. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: Deletions changed plasmid copy number or transfection efficiency, so these data cannot show regulatory elements
The -500 to -300 region is an enhancer that works only in full-length constructs, and -300 to -100 is a repressor site
The -500 to -300 region likely holds a silencer, and -300 to -100 holds needed activator elements
The -500 to -300 region holds the TATA box, and -300 to -100 holds the coding sequence and start codon

rubric: Activity rising when a segment is removed implies negative regulation there, and loss of activity on removing the next segment implies positive elements.
Distractors misassign element roles or dismiss the assay without evidence.

items.prompt: A clinic must genotype one known single-nucleotide variant in 200 patient samples quickly and cheaply, with no need to find new variants. Which approach is best against those criteria?

options.label: Cloning each amplicon into a plasmid and Sanger sequencing several colonies
Allele-specific PCR or a restriction digest of a short amplicon covering the site
Whole-genome sequencing of each sample at 30x coverage to read the site
RNA-seq of each sample to infer the genotype from expression levels

rubric: A targeted PCR-based assay for one known variant is fast, cheap and scalable.
Genome sequencing and cloning cost far more per sample, and RNA-seq does not give reliable genotypes.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to study an essential gene whose complete loss is lethal. The criteria are: keep cells alive long enough to assay, and tune the level of reduction. Which approach is best?

options.label: CRISPR knockout with a frameshift in both alleles of the gene
siRNA or CRISPR interference giving partial, titratable knockdown
Introducing a nonsense mutation into the gene in the germline
Deleting the whole locus by homologous recombination in the cells

rubric: Knockdown reduces expression without eliminating it, so cells survive and levels can be tuned.
The other options aim at complete, permanent loss, which is lethal for an essential gene.

items.prompt: A 3 kb coding sequence will be amplified from cDNA and cloned into an expression vector, and the protein must have the exact native sequence. Which polymerase choice best meets this criterion?

options.label: Taq polymerase, because it has the fastest extension rate on long templates
A proofreading polymerase with 3'-5' exonuclease activity, accepting blunt ends
Taq polymerase, because its 3' A overhang improves the ligation efficiency
Reverse transcriptase alone, because it copies the cDNA with the least error

rubric: Proofreading enzymes have much lower error rates, which is what the sequence-accuracy criterion demands.
Taq lacks proofreading and reverse transcriptase is error-prone, so the others risk mutations.

items.prompt: A student shows that a nuclear extract shifts a labelled promoter fragment in an EMSA and concludes that transcription factor Y binds that sequence specifically. Which critique is most valid?

options.label: The experiment is invalid because EMSA can only be performed with purified protein, never extracts
The shift proves specific binding because any retarded band must come from a single sequence-specific protein
The experiment should have been run denaturing, since native gels destroy protein-DNA complexes
Without competition by excess unlabelled specific versus mutant probe, the shift may be nonspecific binding

rubric: Specificity needs competition controls, or a supershift with antibody against Y, since extracts contain many DNA-binding proteins.
Distractors overstate what a shift shows or misstate how EMSA works.

items.prompt: A group treats cells with a drug and reports a 2-fold increase in gene G expression by RT-qPCR, normalising to reference gene R. Raw data show G's Ct fell by 1 cycle but R's Ct rose by 1 cycle after treatment. What is the most valid critique?

options.label: The fold change is understated, because Ct values cannot be compared across treatments at all
R shifts with treatment, so it is not a valid normaliser and the fold change is unreliable
The result is sound, because any reference gene is automatically valid for every condition
A 1-cycle change in G proves a 10-fold increase, since each cycle is a tenfold difference

rubric: A reference gene that shifts with treatment distorts the delta-delta Ct calculation and needs validation.
Each cycle is about a 2-fold change, and reference genes must be shown stable, not assumed.

items.prompt: A team plans to express a human glycoprotein in E. coli from a genomic clone containing introns. Which concerns are legitimate when judging this plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: Introns will not be spliced out in E. coli, so cDNA is needed
E. coli lacks ribosomes able to translate a eukaryotic mRNA
Rare human codons may limit translation in E. coli
E. coli does not glycosylate proteins in the human pattern
E. coli cannot maintain plasmids carrying human DNA at all

rubric: Missing splicing, absent glycosylation and codon bias are all real limitations of bacterial expression of human proteins.
E. coli ribosomes translate any mRNA with a suitable Shine-Dalgarno site, and plasmids replicate fine with human inserts.

items.prompt: After a stress treatment, steady-state mRNA for gene H doubles. The lab must decide whether this reflects faster transcription or a longer mRNA half-life, and wants one experiment that separates these. Which design best meets that need?

options.label: Sequence the gene H promoter in treated and control cells to look for new mutations that could raise transcription
Measure total mRNA again at several later time points in treated cells only, and fit the rise to a curve
Run a Western blot for the H protein in treated and control cells to see whether protein levels also double
Block new transcription with actinomycin D and compare mRNA decay over time in treated and control cells

rubric: Stopping transcription and following decay measures half-life directly, separating stability from synthesis rate.
Repeat steady-state measures, protein levels or promoter sequence cannot distinguish these mechanisms.

items.prompt: You must amplify a 3 kb genomic fragment for cloning and need the lowest chance of introducing sequence errors into the insert. Which polymerase choice is best, judged by that criterion?

options.label: Taq polymerase, since its faster extension leaves fewer cycles for errors
A proofreading polymerase with 3'→5' exonuclease activity, accepting slower extension
A reverse transcriptase, since it copies templates more accurately than DNA polymerases
Taq polymerase with extra Mg2+, since higher Mg2+ improves base-pairing fidelity

rubric: Proofreading enzymes remove misincorporated bases and give far lower error rates.
Distractors confuse speed or Mg2+ concentration with fidelity; extra Mg2+ actually lowers fidelity.

items.prompt: A colleague argues that because the genetic code is degenerate, synonymous mutations are always functionally neutral. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Correct: the encoded protein is identical, so no step of gene expression can be affected by the change
Wrong: synonymous changes can alter mRNA folding, splicing signals or translation speed, affecting expression
Correct: tRNA abundance is roughly equal across synonymous codons, so translation rates never differ between them
Wrong: synonymous changes alter the amino acid sequence because wobble pairing at the first codon position changes the residue

rubric: Synonymous variants can affect splicing, mRNA stability and translation kinetics.
Distractors wrongly assume protein identity implies no functional effect or equal tRNA pools.

items.prompt: A ChIP-seq experiment shows a transcription factor bound at a promoter, yet knocking out the factor does not change expression of the nearby gene. Which interpretation is best supported, given only these data?

options.label: The knockout probably failed, since binding at a promoter shows the factor is normally an activator of that gene
Binding does not establish regulation; a redundant factor or a nonfunctional binding event may explain it
The gene is likely controlled after transcription instead, which would mean the promoter peak is not real binding
The ChIP peak is probably a false positive, because a factor that truly binds a promoter would change expression

rubric: Occupancy does not equal function; redundancy and nonfunctional binding are common.
Distractors over-infer from either binding or knockout alone.

items.prompt: For quantifying a low-abundance transcript across samples, you need accuracy over a wide dynamic range and must control for sample input differences. Which design best meets these criteria?

options.label: End-point PCR run for 40 cycles, with gel band intensities compared against a loading control band
RT-qPCR with validated reference genes and efficiency-corrected analysis
RT-qPCR normalised only to total RNA mass, assuming equal reverse transcription and amplification efficiency in all samples
Northern blot with one exposure time for all samples, normalised to a loading-control band such as 18S rRNA

rubric: Efficiency-corrected qPCR with validated references gives wide, normalised quantification.
End-point PCR saturates; skipping efficiency checks and Northerns limit range or sensitivity.

items.prompt: You must knock out a gene in human cells with minimal off-target risk, in a clinical-adjacent setting where permanent edits are acceptable. Judging by that criterion, which strategy is the strongest?

options.label: Pick the guide with the highest on-target score alone, since on-target activity scores also predict how specific the guide is genome-wide
Use siRNA against the transcript, since it silences the gene without editing DNA and so carries no risk of off-target genomic cuts
Deliver wild-type Cas9 from a plasmid for long-term expression, since sustained nuclease activity ensures complete knockout of every allele
Choose guides with few predicted off-target sites, use high-fidelity Cas9 as a short-lived RNP, and verify with unbiased off-target assays

rubric: Transient high-fidelity RNP delivery plus guide selection and verification limits off-targets.
Distractors prolong nuclease exposure, ignore specificity, or misstate siRNA as a genomic edit.

items.prompt: You compare CRISPR interference (dCas9-KRAB) with Cas9 knockout for studying an essential gene in cultured cells. Which judgements are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: CRISPRi is unsuitable because dCas9 cannot be directed to promoters
Knockout can produce complete loss, but it may be lethal for an essential gene
CRISPRi allows partial, reversible repression, so cells with an essential gene can stay viable
CRISPRi cuts both DNA strands, so it creates indels at the target

rubric: CRISPRi tunes expression without cutting; knockout gives complete loss that may kill cells.
Distractors misstate that dCas9 cuts DNA or cannot be targeted.

items.prompt: A lab sees that a reporter gene driven by a promoter shows 10-fold higher mRNA after adding a drug, but protein levels rise only 1.5-fold. Polysome profiling shows the mRNA is mostly in light fractions. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: The drug mainly raises transcription, while translation of the mRNA is limited, so protein output lags
The protein is being overproduced and rapidly degraded, which polysome profiling directly shows
The promoter is not responsive, since mRNA increases cannot arise from promoter activity
The drug blocks transcription, and the mRNA seen is from the earlier time point

rubric: Light polysome fractions indicate poor ribosome loading, so translation limits protein.
Distractors contradict the data or claim profiling shows degradation.

items.prompt: Design a system to express a toxic protein only when wanted in E. coli. Constraints: very low basal expression, tight inducibility, and no need for a special host. Which design best meets all?

options.label: A lac promoter with glucose absent from the medium to maximise repression
A T7 promoter in a host with no repressor, relying on low plasmid copy
A strong constitutive promoter on a high-copy plasmid, with the protein tagged for later cleavage
A T7 promoter with lac operator, a host carrying T7 lysozyme (pLysS), and a repressed uninduced state

rubric: T7lac with T7 lysozyme suppresses leaky T7 polymerase activity, giving tight control.
Distractors give constitutive or leaky expression, or reverse glucose catabolite effects.

items.prompt: You need to clone a PCR product into a vector directionally without introducing extra sequence at the junctions and without relying on a unique restriction site inside the insert. Which approach meets these constraints?

options.label: Add the same restriction site to both primer ends so the insert ligates in either orientation
Use overlap-extension homology arms on primers and assemble with Gibson or similar seamless assembly
Blunt-end ligate the product into a single-cut vector, accepting random orientation
Use TA cloning, since the overhang forces one orientation

rubric: Homology-based assembly is directional and scarless and needs no internal sites.
Distractors give random orientation or leave scars or non-directional ligation.

items.prompt: Design a PCR to detect a point mutation (single C→T) in genomic DNA, using standard Taq and gel readout only. Which primer design best discriminates the alleles?

options.label: Primers with the variant in the middle and a lower annealing temperature to boost sensitivity and allele discrimination
Primers flanking the site about 500 bp each side, then compare amplicon sizes on the gel between the two alleles
A primer whose 5' end sits on the variant base, because the 5' end determines where Taq begins extension
Allele-specific primers whose 3' terminal base matches the variant, plus a control amplicon in the same reaction

rubric: A 3' mismatch hampers extension by Taq, giving allele discrimination; a control confirms the reaction.
Distractors misplace the variant or lower stringency, and flanking primers cannot show a point change by size.

items.prompt: Design an experiment to show a distal enhancer is necessary for a gene's expression in its native context, rather than only sufficient in a reporter assay. Which plan fits?

options.label: Delete or silence the enhancer at its endogenous locus and measure target gene expression
Run ChIP-seq for H3K27ac and p300 in the native cell type and call the enhancer necessary from a strong peak at the site
Overexpress the gene from a plasmid lacking the enhancer and test whether the enhancer is still bound by its activators
Clone the enhancer upstream of a minimal promoter and show it drives high luciferase activity in the same cell type

rubric: Necessity needs loss of function at the native locus.
Reporter assays show sufficiency; ChIP and overexpression show only association.

items.prompt: You must test whether a protein binds an RNA motif directly in living cells, capturing only direct contacts at nucleotide resolution. Which approach is best?

options.label: RNA-seq after knockdown of the protein, since changed transcript levels imply direct binding
Formaldehyde crosslinking with ChIP-seq, since it maps protein-nucleic acid contacts in cells
Native RNA immunoprecipitation without crosslinking, since intact complexes show direct contacts
UV crosslinking, immunoprecipitation and sequencing (CLIP) to map crosslink sites

rubric: UV crosslinking captures direct protein-RNA contacts, and CLIP maps them precisely.
Distractors detect indirect effects or no binding information.

items.prompt: Design a bacterial synthetic circuit that reports a transient signal as a stable memory. Which elements would meet this? Select all that apply.

options.label: A promoter induced by signal with a short-lived reporter, which fades when the signal ends
A reporter placed so the flip permanently turns on expression
A signal-induced recombinase that irreversibly flips a promoter or gene
A repressor-free constitutive reporter that is always on

rubric: Recombinase-mediated DNA inversion gives heritable memory of a transient signal.
Distractors lack memory or lack any signal dependence.

items.prompt: A team wants to correct a point mutation in primary cells using Cas9 without making double-strand breaks, since breaks cause indels and p53 activation. They need the single base change with minimal indels. Which design meets this?

options.label: A base editor (deaminase fused to nickase Cas9) with the target base in the editing window
dCas9-KRAB targeted to the mutation site, so the repressed allele is silenced and the base is corrected
Cas9 nuclease with a paired guide RNA and a short oligo, so the target base is replaced by non-homologous end joining
Wild-type Cas9 with a long donor template, relying on homology-directed repair

rubric: Base editors chemically convert a base without double-strand breaks.
Wild-type Cas9 makes breaks; CRISPRi and siRNA do not alter the genome base.
